transcript:
Meeting header
Date: 2026-05-19
Time: 15:00 PDT
Duration: 62 minutes
Attendees: Samir (Redwood AE), Claire (Redwood SE), Diego (Redwood SE), Maya (Stratus Head of ML), Arjun (Stratus SRE), Lucas (Stratus Infra), Priya (Stratus Security)

Summary (auto): deep dive on GPU runtime profiling, comparing TensorRT-LLM and vLLM performance for Stratus IO workloads, plus discussion of CUDA graphs, kernel selection, and deployment constraints for VPC/on-prem.

Transcript: 
[00:00] Samir: hey everyone thanks for joining uh this is samir from redwood i'll hand off to claire and diego for the deep dive, we'll jump into the perf numbers and then go through kernel selection and the cuda graph experiments we ran.
[00:22] Maya: thanks samir, excited — we had some odd throughput drops in our internal tests and want to understand if it's runtime, batching, or model mismatch.
[00:30] Claire: perfect. quick agenda: baseline numbers, tensorRT-LLM vs vLLM comparison, ckpt/quantization notes, cuda graphs and stability, kv cache behavior for long-context chats, and deployment notes for your VPC.
[00:45] Arjun: just to flag security folks on call — priya may jump in on encryption and audit logs.
[00:50] Priya: thanks, will do.
[01:05] Claire: ok baseline: we used Stratus sample set (short/med/long tokens) on an A100 80GB config; vLLM run had lower tail latency for small batch sizes but TensorRT-LLM showed higher peak throughput when using optimized kernels + cuda graphs. numbers: median latency vLLM ~ 42ms for 16-token gen (batch1), TRT-LLM ~ 48ms but throughput at batch16 was ~2.2x TRT vs vLLM. these are rough, we'll share the sheet.
[01:40] Lucas: when you say optimized kernels, are you referring to fused attention kernels?
[01:45] Diego: yeah fused attention, custom matmuls that shrink launch overhead; kernel selection includes deciding whether to use flash attention variants, multi-head vs grouped, and whether we auto-swap to TF32 paths. TRT tends to pick more aggressive fusion.
[02:05] Maya: we saw big spikes when context length grows beyond 2k tokens — is that kv cache thrash?
[02:12] Claire: could be. vLLM's cache management keeps KV on-host and streams, while TRT-LLM variants tend to pin everything in GPU memory and reuse via cuda graphs; if the kv size exceeds reserve that triggers copies. we saw GC-ish pauses when auto-paging happened.
[02:35] Arjun: can you explain the cuda graphs behavior? we tried enabling graphs and saw some correctness issues on variable-length generation.
[02:42] Diego: yeah good point. cuda graphs are fantastic for reducing kernel launch overhead at fixed shapes. they break down with dynamic shapes — e.g., variable decode steps — unless you use the capture/playback pattern carefully. TRT-LLM has a capture wrapper that replays a set of common sequences; for unpredictable lengths you need fallback paths which reduce the wins.
[03:10] Claire: also note that enabling cuda graphs can make profiling harder because the graph hides launches; we attach NVTX ranges inside the graph and record cupti traces.
[03:25] Maya: on quantization — we tested 4-bit q configs and saw degradation in rare token accuracy. what's your recommendation?
[03:32] Samir: tradeoff is model sensitivity vs cost. for retrieval-augmented use cases with short outputs, 4-bit often acceptable; for instruction following or code-gen you might want symmetric 8-bit or quant-aware finetune. also kernel support differs: TRT has optimized kernels for 4/8-bit that vLLM may emulate via quantized matmuls with slight overhead.
[04:00] Lucas: memory footprint concerns — when we enable batching to 32 we ran out of memory with long context. what's the right knob?
[04:08] Claire: there's a few: decrease KV cache retention (time-window), use prefix caching for repeated prefixes, or enable dynamic batching with strict max tokens per batch. also RTT and latency SLOs will constrain max batch. we recommend workload-aware batching: smaller batches for latency-sensitive routes, larger for background batched jobs.
[04:45] Priya: on VPC/on-prem — are there additional constraints for cuda graphs or TRT kernels in private deployments? driver/kernel versions?
[04:52] Diego: yes. TRT kernel versions depend on TensorRT and CUDA driver combos; cuda graphs are part of CUDA runtime; mismatches in driverABI can cause silent fallback. for private deployments we supply a compatibility matrix and a preflight container to validate.
[05:15] Arjun: in our private cluster we run mixed GPU generations (A100 + H100). any gotchas?
[05:22] Claire: heterogeneous clusters complicate kernel selection; TRT may choose kernels optimized for H100 with sm layout that A100 lacks — Redwood's scheduler tags nodes and routes requests by capability; for mixed pools we either pin certain routes to homogeneous pools or use model-variants compiled per GPU family.
[05:45] Maya: can you walk through a concrete profiling trace?
[05:50] Diego: sure — we captured a long decode trace (1.2k tokens). Timeline: token loop overhead (Python/host) ~ 30ms, kernel launches for attention ~ 7-10ms each, KV gather/copy spikes when cache page occurs ~ 200ms pause, cuBLAS matmul runtimes vary with shape. With cuda graphs and TRT optimizations we reduced per-token overhead by ~45% in steady-state because repeated kernels are pre-compiled in the graph.
[06:25] Samir: important note — the wins show up more with larger batch and steady decode; bursty single-token low-latency calls see less improvement.
[06:36] Maya: you mentioned KV paging — how to monitor/avoid it?
[06:40] Claire: instrument host/GPU memory usage and track KV size per request; set per-tenant memory reservations on Dedicated. Redwood monitor alerts on paging events and can fallback to vLLM path which streams KV more aggressively.
[07:05] Arjun: is there a recommended kernel-selection policy? auto or manual?
[07:12] Diego: default auto is good for general workloads. for tight SLOs we recommend manual policy: prefer TRT kernels for throughput routes, prefer vLLM for latency-sensitive or variable-length decoding. You can pin via route config per API key.
[07:35] Lucas: curious about benchmark methodology — what should we run to reproduce your numbers?
[07:40] Claire: run a three-size matrix: batch sizes [1,8,32], context lengths [64,512,2048], model flavors [fp16, int8/4bit]. run both cold-start and warm-cache traces, capture nvprof/cupti, and record tail/median latency and tokens/sec. Redwood will provide a template spreadsheet.
[08:05] Maya: any quick wins we can try today?
[08:08] Samir: reduce batch size for your latency-critical endpoints, enable prefix caching for repeated prompts, and try TRT-LLM with CUDA graphs for background/high-throughput inference. we'll share tuned configs.
[08:20] Priya: sec question — audit logs and KMS for on-prem, is that supported?
[08:25] Samir: yes, for Private we integrate customer KMS/HSM and ship audit logs to your SIEM; we'll share architecture doc.
[08:35] Arjun: you mentioned fallback policies if cuda graphs cause issues — what does that look like?
[08:40] Claire: we instrument graphs at runtime; if we detect CORRUPT or divergence we fallback to baseline runtime (vLLM path or TRT without graphs) for that route and surface an incident. average failover is sub-second but depends on warm-state.
[09:00] Diego: also note some model ops (like certain rotary embedding implementations) have kernel mismatches between TRT and vLLM; we maintain a compatibility list and sometimes rewrite kernels to align numerics.
[09:18] Maya: is there a rule-of-thumb for when to pick TRT-LLM vs vLLM?
[09:22] Claire: TRT-LLM = high throughput, stable shapes, tolerant to aggressive fusion and quantization; vLLM = low-latency, variable-length, better for development and debugging. Many customers use both: TRT routes background/batch traffic, vLLM handles interactive chat.
[09:45] Lucas: if we want deterministic latency and low variance, which should we pick?
[09:49] Diego: vLLM typically gives lower variance at small batch sizes; TRT lowers variance at scale but you need to tune batch shaping and ensure graph capture covers common paths.
[10:10] Claire: quick demo note — we have a lab harness that can replay your traffic shape; we suggest running that in our lab to collect traces.
[10:18] Arjun: about quantization again — are you suggesting QAT for us?
[10:22] Samir: if you need to preserve accuracy for edge tokens, QAT is the safest; post-training quantization can work but we saw some drop on code/instruction tasks. QAT costs more engineering but often pays back in perf.
[10:40] Maya: what's the timeline to get a bench run from Redwood?
[10:44] Samir: we can run baseline within 48 hours after you share samples; deep lab benchmarking with multiple GPU families takes ~1 week.
[10:52] Priya: in that baseline can you include a security checklist for the private deployment?
[10:56] Samir: yes that's part of our standard handoff pack.
[11:05] Claire: quick aside on kernel selection heuristics: we look at shape distribution, compute vs memory bound nature, and numerics sensitivity. we instrument sample batches and run a kernel ablation to pick kernels per op.
[11:25] Lucas: kernel ablation? how automated?
[11:28] Diego: semi-automated; harness iterates kernel variants, measures time and numerical drift. for production we lock to variants that meet perf and accuracy thresholds.
[11:42] Maya: any notable gotchas with CUDA Graphs on multi-tenant Dedicated?
[11:46] Claire: yes: graph capture can hold references to device allocations which complicates memory reclamation in multi-tenant pools; we mitigate with eviction policies and memory padding. also ephemeral graphs per-model-version can increase overhead if not reused.
[12:05] Arjun: curious on metrics — how do you surface per-route token-cost after applying graphs/quant?
[12:10] Samir: Redwood Console shows token-level cost breakdown, kernel-level latency, and a normalized tokens/sec metric per model variant. when you enable graphs we annotate cost savings and projected monthly delta.
[12:28] Maya: any sample numbers on money savings?
[12:31] Samir: for sustained batch workloads we saw up to 35-50% reduction in GPU-hours after switching to TRT+cuda graphs+int8, depending on accuracy tolerance.
[12:45] Priya: ok from security — we need to see SOC2 + the private deploy network diagram and KMS integration points.
[12:52] Samir: will send.
[13:00] Claire: we should talk about profiling artifacts we'll need: nvprof/cupti traces, cublas logs, and system-level psutil dumps.
[13:12] Diego: also include tokenization logs and distribution so we can map shape distributions.
[13:25] Arjun: we can export that.
[13:30] Maya: what about model-variants? do you recompile per quantization level?
[13:35] Claire: yes we build separate deployments per quant profile: fp16, int8, q4 with calibration tables. TRT often requires recalibration and we keep both fp16 and quantized variants during rollouts.
[13:52] Lucas: if we pin routes by API key to a variant, do you have routing fallback if the node pool is full?
[13:58] Diego: yes -- smart routing can fall back to a compatible variant in a different pool (e.g., fp16 on Dedicated) or to hosted endpoints; you can set max-fallback-count in policy.
[14:15] Samir: let's capture concrete next steps: Redwood to kick off baseline perf, share spreadsheet, and propose a lab window.
[14:22] Maya: agreed.
[14:30] Claire: one more perf caveat: TRT kernel numerical differences may slightly change logits leading to tiny differences in top-k; that's why we include A/B evals against your eval set.
[14:45] Maya: we'll include an eval set.
[14:50] Diego: ok final note on monitoring: enable KV eviction metrics and graph-fail counters; we surface when graph re-capture occurs.
[15:00] Arjun: sounds good, thanks.
[15:05] Samir: thanks everyone we'll follow up with the artifacts.

End of transcript.

References: perf spreadsheet (link: drive.redwood/example-perf.xlsx), TRT-LLM runbook (link: docs.redwood/trt-llm-runbook), compatibility matrix (link: docs.redwood/compat-matrix).
